paragraphs: §1 — The argument from the lethal cold of the upper regions, and the universal "all flesh dies" prooftexts

We have already recounted, among the things we recounted of the disagreement of our colleagues (aṣḥābunā), that there are among them those who, on the strength of rational inquiry (bi-l-naẓar), allege that חֲנוֹךְ וְאֵלִיָּהוּ (Enoch and Elijah), upon them be peace, did not ascend to heaven with their bodies, and that this is among the things which the intellects (al-ʿuqūl) hold impossible and which Scripture invalidates. As for the intellect's holding it impossible, in their view, it is because the farther one goes from the earth upward, the more severe the cold grows upon him, until, from the severity of the cold, the body can have no subsistence (qiwām) with it, and so it perishes. But this saying leads to the invalidation of the prophecies and the denial of the miracles, and whoever holds it is obliged not to acknowledge the account of [the ascent].

[As for Scripture invalidating it,] there is His saying [Eccl 3:19] ... הַכֹּל הָיָה מִן הֶעָפָר וְהַכֹּל שָׁב אֶל־הֶעָפָר ("all came from the dust, and all returns to the dust"), and His saying [Ps 89:49] מִי גֶבֶר יִחְיֶה וְלֹא יִרְאֶה מָּוֶת ("what man shall live and not see death?"), [Eccl 3:21 / 7:2] בַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא סוֹף כָּל הָאָדָם ("inasmuch as that is the end of all mankind"), [Ps 146:4] תֵּצֵא רוּחוֹ יָשֻׁב לְאַדְמָתוֹ ("his spirit goes forth, he returns to his dust"), and his saying [Job 30:23] כִּי־בֵית ... מוֹעֵד לְכָל חָי ("for [You will bring me to death, and to] the house of meeting for all the living"), [Job 34:15] יִגְוַע כָּל־בָּשָׂר יַחַד ("all flesh shall perish together").

: The preamble situates the bab within an intra-Karaite controversy already broached "among the things we recounted" — i.e., in Q's earlier survey of the disagreements of aṣḥābunā (probably the sect-and-disagreement material of Maqala I, or an earlier bab of Maqala III). The deniers are rationalists (ahl al-naẓar) who let al-ʿaql override the plain narrative of Gen 5:24 (Enoch) and 2 Kgs 2:11 (Elijah). Q's rejoinder in this clause is the same one he levels against the resurrection-deniers of Bab 8: a position that makes bodily ascent rationally impossible "leads to the invalidation of the prophecies and the denial of the miracles" (ibṭāl al-nubuwwāt wa-inkār al-muʿjizāt) — the muʿjiza by definition suspends the ordinary natural course, so an appeal to ordinary physics (the lethal cold of altitude) cannot bar it. The cosmological premise (cold intensifying with height to a body-destroying degree) reflects the standard ancient meteorology of the sublunar layered atmosphere. : The deniers' scriptural battery is a chain of universal mortality verses (Eccl 3:19; Ps 89:49; Eccl 3:21; Ps 146:4; Job 30:23; Job 34:15). The OCR of p161 is heavily damaged here (the diff-report logs the run as largely "missing" in the Kraken pass and recovered only by the multimodal pass); the verse pointers reconstructed in brackets follow Q's surviving marginal abbreviations (בקהלת, בתהלים, באיוב). The opening of Job 30:23 is lacunose in the source (כִּי־בֵית ... מוֹעֵד), the missing words being כִּי יָדַעְתִּי מָוֶת תְּשִׁיבֵנִי ("for I know You will return me to death"); the surviving phrase is glossed accordingly.
§2 — The universal verses admit of exception; the alternative readings of Ps 89:49

And the like of that of what is in Scripture — these sayings, even though their outward form is the outward form of a generality (ʿumūm), it is not precluded that there be excepted from them the one, the two, and the more; for Scripture does at times employ the generality where a great many are [in fact] excepted from it. That is like His saying [Gen 6:13] כִּי מָלְאָה הָאָרֶץ ... אֹתָם ("for the earth is filled [with violence] through them"), and like [Gen 41:57] וְכָל הָאָרֶץ בָּאוּ מִצְרַיְמָה ("and all the earth came to Egypt"), [Dan 9:11] וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל עָבְרוּ אֶת תּוֹרָתֶךָ ("and all Israel transgressed Your Torah"), and the like of that is beyond counting. And since that is so, His saying [Ps 89:49] מִי גֶבֶר יִחְיֶה וְלֹא יִרְאֶה־מָּוֶת ("what man shall live and not see death?") and what resembles it intends thereby other than the one of whom it is reported that he did not die — namely these two [Enoch and Elijah].

And there may be in that yet another meaning, namely that he intended "who is the one that lives without God's reviving him?" — for he says right after that [Ps 89:49] יְמַלֵּט נַפְשׁוֹ מִיַּד שְׁאוֹל סֶלָה ("[shall he] deliver his soul from the hand of Sheol? Selah"); for he only denied that a human being should save himself and be able to ward [his soul] off from Sheol — but it may well be that God revives him and delivers him from death.

: Q's first and principal answer is the ʿumūm/khuṣūṣ (general/particular) topos of Arabic legal hermeneutics: a grammatically universal statement (kullu, "all," "every man") routinely tolerates unstated exceptions. He documents the point with three Scriptural "all"-statements that are patently non-exhaustive (Gen 6:13; Gen 41:57's "all the earth came to Egypt"; Dan 9:11's "all Israel transgressed"). The dialectical payoff: Ps 89:49's "what man shall live and not see death?" is a rhetorical generality from which the two reported non-diers (Enoch, Elijah) are simply the excepted cases — so the verse does not bar their deathless ascent. This is the same exegetical instrument Q wields against the resurrection-deniers' universal "no-return" verses in Bab 8 §2–3. : A second, alternative construal of Ps 89:49, hinging on its continuation (89:49b, יְמַלֵּט נַפְשׁוֹ מִיַּד שְׁאוֹל): the verse denies only self-rescue from death — no man can, by his own power, deliver his soul from Sheol — leaving open that God may revive or deliver whomever He wills. So even read strictly, the verse is no obstacle. The clause is textually fragile: the diff-report flags several question-marked readings here (מנעها, מן, שׁאול, ويفلته من الموت), but the sense is secure from the cited Hebrew lemma.
§5 — The mechanism of the bodily ascent: exchange of the gross body, then stripping of corporeality; the angelic analogy

And after we have said that חֲנוֹךְ וְאֵלִיָּהוּ (Enoch and Elijah) ascended to heaven with their bodies, we have need to make plain how that was. So we say: each one of the two went up with his body to heaven; and when he reached there, God stripped that body from him and clothed him in a body subtler (alṭaf) than it — since that first body was an earthly, dense (kathīf) body that would perish in the piercing of the body of the sphere (jirm al-falak), whereas the second, subtle body is not so. And when he came to be in the highest [part] of the sphere, He stripped from him corporeality (al-jurmiyya) altogether, and he became a bare, spiritual substance (jawharan mujarradan rūḥāniyyan).

And that is the counterpart of what He does with the angels when He wishes to dispatch one of them to the earth: He clothes him in a subtle heavenly body (jurman samāwiyyan laṭīfan), and clothes that heavenly body in an earthly body, so that he may descend to the lower [region]; then He sends him to whomever He wills, until, when he has delivered the message, He strips from him the earthly body. And when it is removed from him, he rises by the nature of the heavenly body to heaven, until, when he has come to be there, he is divested of his heavenly body and passes into the world of the intellect (ʿālam al-ʿaql).

: Having dispatched the deniers' objections, Q turns constructive (§5; the intervening markers §3–§4 are lost to the page's OCR damage, but the surviving Arabic numeral here is "5"). His account of the ascent is a graduated de-materialization: (1) the gross "earthly, dense" body cannot survive "the piercing of the body of the sphere" (kharq jirm al-falak) — the same cold-and-density physics the deniers invoked, now conceded at the natural level; (2) so at the firmament God exchanges it for a subtle (laṭīf) celestial body; (3) at the sphere's summit even that is stripped, and the person becomes a "bare, spiritual substance" (jawhar mujarrad rūḥānī) — i.e., a pure intellect. The vocabulary (kathīf/laṭīf, jurmiyya, jawhar mujarrad, ʿālam al-ʿaql) is Neoplatonizing rather than strictly Bahshamī kalām, and is notable in a writer usually so close to ʿAbd al-Jabbār; it aligns Q here with the Neoplatonic-Muʿtazilī ascent-cosmology current in 10th-century Iraq. : The angelic analogy seals the mechanism: angelic descent is by successive clothing (a subtle heavenly jurm, then an earthly jurm over it) and angelic re-ascent by successive unclothing (shedding the earthly body, rising by the nature of the celestial body, then shedding that too to reach ʿālam al-ʿaql). Enoch and Elijah's ascent is the mirror image — they go up clothed in the gross body, which is then progressively exchanged and shed. The two-garment angelology (a luminous body sheathed in a gross one for terrestrial mission) is a widespread medieval motif; Q deploys it to render bodily ascent both real (the deniers are wrong) and physically intelligible (the gross body does not, after all, survive the upper regions — it is transformed). This is the closing argument of the bab and of Maqala III.

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading is explicit: ʿalā man zaʿama anna Ḥanōkh wa-Ēliyyāhū lam yaṣʿadā ilā al-samāʾ bi-ajsāmihimā — "against whoever alleged that Enoch and Elijah did not ascend to heaven with their bodies." The adversaries are not Christians (the target of Babs 1–7) nor an unnamed sect, but Q's own aṣḥābunā (Karaite colleagues) of a rationalist bent who let al-naẓar override the narratives of Gen 5:24 and 2 Kgs 2:11. The dispute is thus intra-Karaite, fitting the eschatology-and-cosmology block of the later babs of Maqala III. Q's own position is firmly for the literal, bodily ascent — the same anti-deniers stance, and the same defense of muʿjiza against naturalistic objection, he takes in Bab 8 against the resurrection-deniers.

- The shared argumentative apparatus with Bab 8. This bab is the structural twin of Bab 8 (resurrection): an opponent invokes (i) rational impossibility and (ii) universal mortality verses; Q replies that (i) the impossibility-argument "leads to the invalidation of the prophecies and the denial of the miracles," and (ii) the universal verses admit of exception (ʿumūm tolerating istithnāʾ). The Ps 89:49 treatment here — read first as a generality-with-exception and then, alternatively, as denying only self-deliverance from Sheol — closely parallels the Bab 8 §3 handling of the deniers' "no-return" prooftexts.

- The de-materialization cosmology (§5). The constructive core is unusual for Q: a three-stage ascent (gross earthly body → subtle celestial body → bare spiritual substance in ʿālam al-ʿaql), mirrored by the two-garment angelology. The kathīf/laṭīf gradation, the jawhar mujarrad rūḥānī, and the "world of the intellect" are Neoplatonic-Muʿtazilī rather than Bahshamī-kalām vocabulary; the passage is a good witness to the Neoplatonic admixture in 10th-century Karaite-Muʿtazilī cosmology. Note that Q here concedes the deniers' physics at the natural level (the dense body could not survive "the piercing of the sphere") and rescues the miracle precisely by positing divine bodily exchange — the cold does not falsify the ascent; it explains why the body had to be transformed.

- Textual condition and the Bab 24/25 boundary. As the edition's notes warn, the Bab 24/25 region is delicate: the file's opening lines (through the נִשְׁבַּע/וְזָרְחָה cluster) are the tail of Bab 24 and are excluded; Bab 25 begins at the الباب الخامس وعشرين heading on p161. The Hebrew citations on p161 are badly garbled in the Kraken pass and were recovered by the multimodal pass (62 logged disagreements); the verse pointers in brackets follow Q's surviving marginal abbreviations. The section numbering is defective: only the Arabic markers transcribed as "2" (the lacunose "...2..." after the impossibility argument) and "5" (before the mechanism passage) survive; §§3–4 are lost in the page damage. There is no lacuna of content at the bab's end — it concludes naturally with the angelic analogy, immediately after which p159 opens with the maqala-closing doxology.

- How Maqala III ends. The maqala terminates at the top of p159 with the formula وَهذَا آخِرُ المَقالَةِ الثَّالِثَةِ والحمدُ لله ربِّ العَالَمين وَتِلْوَهَا المَقالةُ الرابعة في الوُجُوه والأَسْبابِ التي يُوَصَّل بها إلى مَعْرِفَةِ الفَرائض — "This is the end of the Third Maqala; praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds. Following it is the Fourth Maqala, on the means and causes by which one arrives at the knowledge of the commandments." The Fourth Maqala's preamble (the four-tier classification of humankind into the People of pure Obedience, the צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים; the lowest tier, the הָרְשָׁעִים גְּמוּרִים; and two intermediate tiers) then begins — all excluded here as next-maqala material.
